lead.headline: The US sets a 25% tariff on Indian goods, the second-highest of 14 countries, but says it falls to 17% if a trade deal is signed
lead.short: The US Trade Representative on Wednesday announced a 25% tariff on goods from India over what it called "unreasonable acts, policies, and practices" that burden US commerce. Among the 14 economies hit, only Vietnam, at 35%, faces a higher rate than India. The USTR said the rate could drop to 17% once the two countries sign a trade agreement.

why.text: It puts a number on what India's exporters face, and makes the stalled trade deal worth eight percentage points.

more: The order says the 25% is net of existing tariffs, so it will not add to the 10% "forced labour" duty already in effect, though the USTR can still adjust it. It follows two Section 301 investigations, into forced labour and industrial overcapacity. China faces up to 40%, and the rest of the 14, including the EU, Japan and South Korea, face 20% or 25%.

India's commerce ministry said it had taken note and the notice was under examination. "India engaged constructively throughout this investigation," it said, adding that India had told the US it does not have structural excess capacity in any sector, and that the two countries are negotiating a bilateral trade agreement.

update.new: The US sets India's rate at 25%.
update.front: The tariffs are now announced: 25% on India.

seconds.headline: The Supreme Court cancels Anand Mohan's early release in the 1994 killing of an IAS officer, and orders him back to jail within a month
seconds.short: The Supreme Court on Thursday quashed the premature release of former MP Anand Mohan, who was serving a life sentence for the 1994 murder of Gopalganj district magistrate G. Krishnaiah, and ordered Bihar to ensure he surrenders within a month. It struck down the state's remission notification as arbitrary. "Article 21 cannot be a one-sided guarantee," the bench said.

why.text: It tells states they cannot change prison rules to free a favoured convict, and puts victims' rights into the remission decision.

more: A bench headed by Justice Dipankar Datta said the right to life under Article 21 extends beyond the convict to the victims, their families and society at large. It found Bihar's sudden departure from its earlier remission policy indefensible and unreasonable, and said the sole test for early release cannot be that a convict "showed signs of reform".

Mohan, a gangster-turned-politician from Bihar, walked out of Saharsa jail on 27 April after Bihar amended its prison rules. Krishnaiah's wife, Uma Krishnaiah, challenged the release. The court said any future attempt at remission in the case must give her a hearing.

seconds.headline: At least 31 people are killed and 21 injured when a fuel tanker overturns and bursts into flames on a Cairo highway
seconds.short: Thirty-one people were killed and 21 injured in a huge fire on a busy ring road in Cairo's Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry said. State media reported that the tanker overturned and doused nearby vehicles with petrol. Footage showed flames and black smoke towering into the night sky.

why.text: It is one of Egypt's deadliest road disasters in years, in a city where emergency help is often slow to arrive.

more: The tanker, owned by a private contractor, lost control when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, Al-Ahram reported, citing sources close to the investigation. It crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire. Several nearby vehicles were torched. Hospitals nearby treated people for burns and smoke inhalation, and a large crowd gathered once the fire was out.

The regional public prosecutor has opened an investigation and asked for DNA samples to be taken from the dead. Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, as informal housing, run-down infrastructure and slow emergency response make them more common and harder to fight, even in the capital.

seconds.headline: Kim Jong Un shows off five types of nuclear warhead and says North Korea will never give up its arsenal, after snubbing Trump
seconds.short: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un inspected nuclear warheads and a plant making bomb material, state media reported on Thursday, vowing never to change the country's status as a nuclear-armed state. "Our nuclear capability has now become a reality," he said. It was his most direct message to the US since Donald Trump floated a meeting last week.

why.text: It ends talk of a quick Trump-Kim summit and shows an arsenal still growing, a day after Pyongyang expelled a Swiss diplomat.

more: Photos released by the state news agency showed metal casings of five separate designs, including a "super-large" warhead. "This is the greatest number of nuclear warhead types we've seen in a single North Korean image," said Ankit Panda of the Carnegie Endowment. He said Kim is not interested in denuclearisation but wants a new bargain with the US.

Kim accused Washington of approving South Korea's push for a nuclear-powered submarine. The UN nuclear watchdog's head, Rafael Grossi, warned a week ago that Pyongyang was expanding its uranium enrichment. Trump met Kim three times in his first term; he said this time it was "not really the right time."

update.front: Kim has now put his warheads on show.

stories.headline: The UK and EU publish their reset treaties, and the food deal carries a 10-year exit clause that would make the quitter pay
stories.short: Britain and the EU are publishing two of the treaties agreed last week in their post-Brexit reset, on food trade and emissions trading, along with a bill to put the deal into law. The BBC understands the food deal has a 10-year termination clause: a side that quits would pay to rebuild the border checks being dismantled.

why.text: The clause makes the deal costly to undo, just as Badenoch promises to scrap it and Farage says he would not pay.

more: Food exporters stand to gain most from the scrapping of red tape and border facilities, and an internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports. Industry insiders say shoppers may see no clear change at the checkout, partly because of the energy price shock from war in the Middle East.

"The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements," said European affairs minister Hamish Falconer. "It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes." The third text, on the youth experience scheme, comes later.

update.new: The treaty texts and their exit clause.

stories.headline: Tata Trusts take Tata Sons to the Bombay High Court to block N. Chandrasekaran's third term as chairman
stories.short: Tata Trusts, which own 66% of Tata Sons, have filed two suits in the Bombay High Court challenging the reappointment of N. Chandrasekaran as chairman of the group's holding company. The board approved his third term, from February 2027, by a majority vote on 17 September. The Trusts call it illegal. The hearing is on Friday.

why.text: India's biggest business group is now fighting over who runs it in court, not the boardroom.

more: The Trusts say the reappointment breaks Tata Sons' Articles of Association, and want it declared invalid. Sir Dorab Tata Trust is seeking ₹50 crore in damages and Sir Ratan Tata Trust ₹15 crore, with 18% interest. The suits name Tata Sons and six directors, including Noel Tata. Abhishek Manu Singhvi represents the Trusts.

They also want Chandrasekaran barred from using his casting vote at the board meeting on 30 November if the Trusts' nominees split again. The suits were first mentioned before a judge who recused himself, and the matter was then mentioned before Justice Abhay Ahuja, who set the hearing for 3pm on Friday.

stories.headline: The rupee closes at an eight-month high of 92.23 a dollar and wipes out this year's losses, as strategists see room for more
stories.short: The rupee closed at 92.2337 a dollar on Wednesday, its strongest in eight months, as most other Asian currencies weakened, extending a November rally fuelled by record foreign buying of Indian shares and lower oil prices. ANZ sees room for it to reach 90 to 91, and ICICI Securities Primary Dealership expects at least 91.

why.text: A stronger rupee makes imports, oil and foreign travel cheaper, and gives the RBI a chance to rebuild its reserves.

more: The swift rebound from near-record lows last month lets the Reserve Bank recoup foreign exchange reserves, which have fallen more than $80 billion from their September peak. Its record $239.2 billion short forward book adds to the case for buying dollars, but strategists say it may wait. Barclays recommends a bet on the rupee targeting 89.53.

"A slightly prolonged period of appreciation in the rupee could be a necessary condition for hedging behavior to be altered," said Sakshi Gupta of HDFC Bank. Exporters sold about $15 billion in the forward market in the first 20 days of November. On Thursday the Sensex was flat at about 83,900 at 2pm.

update.new: The rupee hits an eight-month high.

notes.USD/INR: About 92.4 a dollar, after an eight-month high on Wednesday.

stories.headline: The US approves SpaceX's plan for up to a million satellites to run AI data centres in orbit, the first approval of its kind
stories.short: The US Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX's plan to put up to a million satellites into orbit to process data for artificial intelligence, powered by sunlight. The project, called Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy", the FCC said. Separately, Elon Musk pledged two SpaceX shares to every child in the US.

why.text: AI's hunger for computing is now reaching into space, as communities across America push back against data centres on the ground.

more: Under the licence, deployment must begin by November 2033, with 10% up by November 2035 and half by November 2038. SpaceX wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. They will fly between 500km and 2,000km up and relay data to Earth through Starlink, which already has more than 10,000 satellites. It is unclear whether all million will be launched.

"This will be a great asset to America and the world," Musk wrote on X. FCC chairman Brendan Carr said it "opens a bold new frontier". Musk's share pledge, worth more than $18 billion, gives each child one share from the company and one from him personally.

stories.headline: Nvidia stops server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, and a second executive romance comes to light
stories.short: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers with its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times reported. Partners such as Supermicro and Dell told buyers in the four countries that Nvidia would not allow their orders to ship. It follows the US blacklisting of Megaspeed, suspected of diverting AI chips to China.

why.text: The scandal over AI chips leaking to China is now reshaping where Nvidia will sell, days after Huang's return.

more: Huang was not the only Nvidia executive in a relationship with someone at a customer, according to a report carried by the Hindustan Times. His longtime lieutenant Jay Puri dated Cenly Chen, a senior executive at Super Micro, for years while the server maker competed for Nvidia's chips. The two married in Big Sur, California, on 7 March.

"I never had to rely on personal relationships for professional gain," Chen said. Puri recently stepped aside as head of Nvidia's global sales. In March the Justice Department charged a Super Micro co-founder, a sales manager and a broker with conspiring to smuggle more than $500 million of servers into China.

stories.headline: Europe's Hera probe shows NASA's DART spacecraft gouged a stadium-sized crater in the asteroid it struck four years ago
stories.short: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has sent back the first close-up images of the scar left on the asteroid Dimorphos by NASA's DART mission, which deliberately crashed into it in 2022. The car-sized impactor carved out a crater the size of a stadium, nearly as big as the 151-metre asteroid itself, ESA said on Wednesday.

why.text: It is the first close look at whether humanity could knock a dangerous asteroid off course, and how.

more: DART hit Dimorphos at more than 6 kilometres a second in September 2022, releasing about 10 billion joules of energy and shortening its 12-hour orbit around a larger asteroid, Didymos, by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most cautious forecast. The pair pose no risk to Earth, and are about 193 million kilometres away.

"We knew right away that the impact was successful, that DART made a really, really large mess," said Sabina Raducan of the International Space Science Institute in Bern. "However, we didn't really know what kind of mess." Scientists had expected either a crater or a reshaped asteroid, said Patrick Michel, Hera's principal investigator.
